issues.legal_issue: A rule prescribing the method for valuing residential property for wealth-tax purposes is procedural and evidentiary when it selects a recognized method without changing the underlying tax liability.
material_facts: The rule prescribed a formula for valuing houses wholly or mainly used for residential purposes, based on net maintainable rent.
The formula used a recognized method of valuation and was intended to promote uniformity and avoid disparities in valuing similar properties.
The statutory charge to wealth tax arose independently of the method used to determine an asset’s value.
issues.conclusion: The valuation rule is essentially procedural and evidentiary, not substantive.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished provisions imposing tax liability from machinery provisions that quantify it, and substantive law from procedural law. Section 3 of the Wealth Tax Act imposed the charge, while Section 7(1) provided for valuation subject to rules made under Section 46. The rule selected a recognized method of valuation and did not alter substantive rights or create a new liability. The Court relied on Maxwell v. Murphy, Republic of Costa Rica v. Erlanger, Izhar Ahmad Khan v. Union of India, Kesoram Industries and Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Commissioner of Wealth Tax, and the general distinction between charging and machinery provisions.

rule.if: wealth_tax_valuation_proceeding and residential_property_valuation and rule_prescribes_recognized_valuation_method and method_does_not_change_tax_liability

predicates.wealth_tax_valuation_proceeding: The proceeding determines the value of an asset for the purpose of assessing wealth tax.
predicates.residential_property_valuation: The asset being valued is a house used wholly or mainly for residential purposes.
predicates.rule_prescribes_recognized_valuation_met: The rule specifies a method of valuation that is recognized for property of that kind.
predicates.method_does_not_change_tax_liability: The method determines how an asset is valued without changing the underlying liability to tax.

issues.definition: When a wealth-tax valuation proceeding concerns residential property and a rule selects a recognized valuation method without changing the tax liability, the rule is procedural and evidentiary.

issues.legal_issue: A procedural rule governing the valuation of property applies to proceedings that are pending when the rule comes into force.
material_facts: The assessments concerned earlier valuation years, but the assessments in the representative cases were made after the valuation rule had been introduced.
The assessees sought use of the rule’s valuation method, and the dispute over its application proceeded through appeals and references.
The rule governed the method of valuation rather than creating or altering the underlying tax liability.
issues.conclusion: The valuation rule applies to pending proceedings, including proceedings concerning earlier valuation years.
issues.legal_principle: Procedural provisions generally apply to pending proceedings because a litigant has no vested right in procedure; provisions affecting existing substantive rights are not applied retrospectively without express enactment or necessary intendment. The Court relied on Jose Da Costa v. Bascora Sadasiva Sinai Narpomim, Associated Cement Company Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer, Kota, and the principles stated in Halsbury’s Laws of England and Bennion’s Statutory Interpretation. It also applied its conclusion that the valuation rule was procedural and evidentiary.

predicates.pending_wealth_tax_valuation_proceeding: A proceeding to assess wealth tax or determine an asset’s value was pending when the valuation rule came into force.
predicates.rule_governs_valuation_method: The rule prescribes how an asset’s value is to be determined in the proceeding.
predicates.rule_does_not_alter_substantive_rights: The rule changes the procedure for determining value without changing an existing substantive right or liability.

issues.definition: A pending wealth-tax valuation proceeding is governed by a valuation-method rule that does not alter substantive rights.
